title: Student Loan Borrowers Sue Trump Administration Over Credit Report Debt Forgiveness Errors
body:
A coalition of former student‑loan borrowers has filed a federal lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Education, alleging that the agency’s handling of their forgiven debt has caused lasting financial harm. The plaintiffs contend that, despite receiving official loan discharge under the 2017 “borrower defense” rule, the loans continue to appear on their credit reports as active obligations, dragging down credit scores, inflating interest‑rate costs on new credit and, in some cases, prompting collection actions. The suit, lodged in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, seeks monetary damages, a court order compelling the department to correct the credit‑reporting errors, and a declaration that the agency’s practices violate federal consumer‑protection statutes.

The borrowers’ grievance centers on a technical flaw that emerged after the Education Department’s 2017 policy change, which allowed borrowers who had been defrauded by for‑profit colleges to have their federal loans discharged. While the Department issued discharge letters and notified the three major credit bureaus—Equifax, Experian and TransUnion—many of the borrowers discovered that the loans remained listed as “in repayment” or “charged‑off” for months, and in some instances years, after the discharge. The plaintiffs argue that the lingering entries have led to lower credit scores, higher insurance premiums, and denied rental applications, effectively negating the financial relief the discharge was meant to provide.

Legal experts note that the case raises complex questions about the intersection of federal loan‑forgiveness programs and private‑sector credit‑reporting practices. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), credit bureaus are required to maintain accurate information and to correct errors when notified. However, the plaintiffs argue that the Department’s failure to provide timely, definitive data to the bureaus amounts to a “failure to furnish” required information, leaving the bureaus with outdated records that they are not obligated to update. “When the government says a debt is gone, it should be gone in every system that tracks that debt,” said Karen Liu, a consumer‑rights attorney who is not representing the plaintiffs. “If the Department’s own paperwork is inconsistent, borrowers are left to fight a bureaucratic maze to protect their credit.”

The lawsuit also invokes the Administrative Procedure Act, claiming that the Education Department’s implementation of the borrower‑defense rule lacked proper notice and comment, and that the agency’s subsequent handling of credit‑reporting data was arbitrary and capricious. The plaintiffs point to internal Department memos obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request, which suggest that staff were aware of the reporting glitches but did not prioritize remediation, citing limited resources and competing policy initiatives. The suit therefore seeks not only individual relief but also systemic reform, urging the Department to establish a standardized protocol for communicating loan discharges to credit bureaus and to audit its records for lingering inaccuracies.

If the court sides with the borrowers, the implications could be far‑reaching. A ruling that mandates the Department to proactively correct credit reports could trigger a wave of similar lawsuits from other categories of federal debtors, including those whose loans were discharged under the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program or the recent COVID‑19 relief measures. Moreover, a precedent that holds a federal agency accountable for third‑party reporting errors could pressure other government bodies—such as the Internal Revenue Service and the Social Security Administration—to tighten data‑sharing practices with private entities.

The Department of Education has responded with a brief statement, asserting that it “takes the accuracy of credit reporting seriously” and that it is “reviewing the plaintiffs’ allegations.” No comment was offered on the merits of the case or on any anticipated timeline for corrective action. As the lawsuit proceeds, borrowers who believe they have been similarly affected are being urged to monitor their credit reports, dispute erroneous entries directly with the bureaus, and consider joining the litigation if they meet the class‑action criteria. The outcome of this case could shape how federal debt relief programs are administered and how their benefits are reflected in the broader financial ecosystem, offering a crucial test of accountability for government‑managed consumer data.
